clue.text: Finishes off letter, most annoyed

parts.note: a handwritten t is only complete once its stroke is put through it, so to finish it off is to cross it: crosses
T is simply a letter of the alphabet, the one whose writing is finished by crossing

explanation.surface: Someone completing a letter in a temper, at their most irritated.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'crossing your t's' hides inside the clue: 'Finishes off letter' reads as CROSSES T, run together into one word.
explanation.definitionFit: Cross means angry or irritated, so its superlative is a direct synonym for most annoyed.

clue.text: Cloth cape used by the French at rugby, oddly

parts.note: C is the map abbreviation for cape
le is French for the

indicators.note: oddly says the letters in odd positions, first, third and fifth, are taken

explanation.surface: A cape worn by French rugby players, strangely.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the cloth' is a collective term for clergy, as in a man of the cloth.
explanation.definitionFit: The cloth is an idiom for the clergy as a body, from their distinctive dress.

clue.text: Away from home supporter finds abuse welcome

parts.note: someone away from home is out
a stay is a prop or support, such as a rope steadying a mast

explanation.surface: A fan at an away match finds the reception is hostile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'supporter' looks like a fan, but it is a stay, a prop or rope that holds something up.
explanation.definitionFit: To outstay your welcome is to impose on hosts by lingering too long, so the verb means abusing hospitality.

clue.text: Work to teach group of killers caution?

parts.note: killer whales swim in groups called schools
in football a player cautioned by the referee is booked

explanation.surface: A task to educate a gang of murderers about being careful.
explanation.walkthrough: The killers are killer whales, hence the question mark; a caution is a booking, as in football.
explanation.definitionFit: A school book is a textbook, a written work used for teaching pupils.

clue.text: Achieves entry after arranging time for affairs?

indicators.note: after arranging says the letters only make the answer once they have been put in a new order

explanation.surface: Someone gets into a place after organising a time for some business.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affairs' reads as business but means extramarital flings; the question mark flags the jokey definition.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is the supposed urge to stray that strikes after several years of marriage, a period ripe for infidelity.

clue.text: German cycle-maker has not done without English backing

indicators.note: backing means the assembled letters are read from the end to the start
without in its old sense of outside: the uncooked word goes round the English abbreviation

parts.note: meat not done is underdone or raw

explanation.surface: A German bicycle manufacturer has failed to secure English sponsorship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without' is used in its old sense of outside, and 'backing' turns the whole result round. The cycle is not a bicycle but the Ring, a cycle of four operas.
explanation.definitionFit: Richard Wagner composed The Ring of the Nibelung, a cycle of four operas, so he is literally a maker of a cycle.

clue.text: Modern-day houses to live, being retired

indicators.note: houses means the date abbreviation takes the verb inside it, like a home

parts.note: AD, anno domini, marks the modern era of dates
to be is to exist or live

explanation.surface: Contemporary homes to live in, now that one has stopped working.
explanation.walkthrough: 'retired' looks like stopping work but means gone to bed.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has retired for the night has gone to bed, so is in bed.

clue.text: College confused when cuts upset staff

indicators.note: cuts means the jumbled word slices into the middle of the reversed one
upset in a down clue means turned upside down, so read backwards

parts.note: to staff a post is to man it

indicators.note: confused says the letters of the next word are muddled

explanation.surface: A college in chaos when cutbacks distress its employees.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' reverses the staff word to NAM; 'confused' scrambles the time word to NEWH, which 'cuts' into it. Newnham is a Cambridge college.
explanation.definitionFit: Newnham is a college of Cambridge University, founded for women.

clue.text: Cavalier chap on a roll

indicators.note: in a down clue on means the first piece sits on top of the rest

parts.note: Roy is a man's name, so a chap
a roll is a list of names, as in a roll call

explanation.surface: A man riding a winning streak with a dashing manner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cavalier' looks like an adjective for casual, but with its capital it is a Civil War supporter of King Charles I.
explanation.definitionFit: In the English Civil War the Cavaliers were the supporters of King Charles I, so royalists.

clue.text: Small amphibian first to leave port

indicators.note: first to leave says the opening letter of the synonym departs from it

parts.note: port is the left-hand side of a ship

explanation.surface: A tiny newt is the first creature to abandon the harbour.
explanation.walkthrough: 'port' looks like a harbour, but it is the nautical word for left.
explanation.definitionFit: An eft is a young newt, a small amphibian found in crossword grids far more than in conversation.

clue.text: Hard hail coming, biting easterly sure at first to prevail

parts.note: H is the pencil abbreviation for hard
ave is a Latin greeting, a hail

indicators.note: biting means one piece takes the others into its mouth, so they go inside it

parts.note: something coming is on its way, run together as on way
E is the abbreviation for east, so easterly

indicators.note: at first says only the opening letter of the next word is taken

explanation.surface: A hard hailstorm is approaching, the east wind making sure it wins out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'biting' takes the east letter and the first of 'sure' inside the phrase for coming, while 'at first' picks the S. Ave is Latin for hail.
explanation.definitionFit: To get your own way is to win the argument, which is an idiom for prevailing.

clue.text: Apparently books he intercepts belonging to computer expert?

indicators.note: intercepts means the books and he cut in between the letters of the following phrase

parts.note: of shows possession, belonging to
NT is the New Testament, the books of the Christian Bible's second part
taken as written
an expert is an ace, so a computer expert is an ace of IT, information technology

explanation.surface: Seemingly the reading material is snatched by a tech whizz.
explanation.walkthrough: 'intercepts' splits the possessive phrase after its first letter. The question mark flags the whimsical 'ace of IT' for a computer expert.
explanation.definitionFit: Something true on the face of it is so going by appearances, an idiom meaning apparently.

clue.text: Do finally persuade couple when talking

parts.note: to win someone over to your view is to get round them

indicators.note: when talking says the next word is to be taken as it sounds when spoken

parts.note: a couple is two

explanation.surface: Coax a pair of people while having a chat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Do finally' is a verb phrase, matching the phrasal verb: to get round to something is to do it at last.
explanation.definitionFit: To get round to a task is an idiom for eventually doing it after delay.

clue.text: Seeds being split leads to draw having appealing look

indicators.note: the leads of the following words are their opening letters, which are taken in order

explanation.surface: A drawing having an attractive appearance.
explanation.walkthrough: Indian dhal is made from split pulses such as lentils, which are seeds, so the definition describes the dish's ingredient.
explanation.definitionFit: Dhal is the Indian name for split pulses, the dried seeds of lentils, peas or beans, split for cooking.

clue.text: Perhaps the Scottish cease to like our Chairman's advisers

parts.words: Perhaps the Scottish cease to like
parts.note: to go off something is to cease to like it, and in Scots go is gang, so gang off is how a Scot might say it
taken as written

explanation.surface: Maybe Scots stop being fond of our leader's counsellors.
explanation.walkthrough: The Chairman is Chairman Mao; the Gang of Four were the radical group around him in China's Cultural Revolution.
explanation.definitionFit: The Gang of Four were the four leading Communist officials around Mao Zedong, the Chairman, during his last years.

clue.text: A couple of runs are so long! .

indicators.note: a couple of means the piece is written down twice in a row

parts.note: in cricket a bye is a run scored when the ball passes the batsman untouched

explanation.surface: Someone exclaiming that two runs take an age.
explanation.walkthrough: A bye is a cricket run taken without the bat touching the ball; 'so long!' reads as an exclamation about time but is a farewell.
explanation.definitionFit: So long is an informal way to say goodbye, as is the reduplicated farewell.

clue.text: Theologian finding answer in reflective classroom subjects

indicators.note: in tells us the single letter is placed within the reversed school subjects
reflective says the subjects appear as in a mirror, read backwards

parts.note: sums, arithmetic, is a primary-school subject
RE is Religious Education, a school subject in Britain

explanation.surface: A theologian works out the answer while pondering what is taught in schools.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reflective' gives ERSMUS, and 'in' sets the answer abbreviation inside it. Religious Education is a compulsory British school subject.
explanation.definitionFit: Erasmus of Rotterdam was a Dutch Renaissance humanist and theologian.

clue.text: Civil rights came with bail

indicators.note: rights as a verb means sets straight, so the mixed letters are put into proper order

explanation.surface: Civil liberties arrived along with release on bail.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rights' looks like a noun after 'Civil', but as a verb (sets straight) it is the anagram signal for the two words after it.
explanation.definitionFit: Civil means polite and courteous, the same as friendly or amicable.

clue.text: No harm dissembling about accepted amount of effort

indicators.note: about means the rearranged letters go around the single letter
dissembling, pretending, suggests the letters disguise themselves by changing order

parts.note: U stands for upper-class and so socially acceptable

explanation.surface: No harm in pretending to go along with the agreed workload.
explanation.walkthrough: 'dissembling' rearranges NO HARM to MANHOR, and 'about' puts U (upper-class, so socially accepted) inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: A man-hour is a unit of work, the effort one person puts in over an hour.

clue.text: In no way upset, stick with it

indicators.note: in a down clue upset means turned upside down, reading the word backwards

parts.note: a baton is a stick, such as a conductor's or relay runner's

explanation.surface: Not distressed at all, carry on with it.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' looks like part of 'In no way upset' but it turns BATON over to NOTAB.
explanation.definitionFit: Not a bit is an emphatic idiom for not at all, meaning in no way.

clue.text: Country areas limit long rambling

indicators.note: limit means the two letters form the boundaries on either side of the jumbled word

parts.note: A is the abbreviation for area, and the plural gives two of them
A is the abbreviation for area, and the plural gives two of them

indicators.note: rambling, wandering about, suggests the letters stray from their order

explanation.surface: A country's regions cap how far you can go on a long hike.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rambling' turns LONG into NGOL, and 'limit' sets an A, from 'areas', at each end of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Angola is a country in south-west Africa.

clue.text: US town making pork pie with a butter filling

indicators.note: filling means the pieces go inside the untruth, like stuffing in a pie

parts.note: pork pie is Cockney rhyming slang for lie, often shortened to porky
a ram butts with its head, so it is a butter

explanation.surface: A US town producing a meat pie filled with dairy fat.
explanation.walkthrough: 'butter' is not the dairy spread but a thing that butts. Pork pie is British rhyming slang for a lie.
explanation.definitionFit: Laramie is a town in Wyoming, United States.

clue.text: Cry "oh", quietly over the moon

indicators.note: over means everything is turned round, read upwards in a down clue

parts.note: to sob is to cry
taken as written
P is piano, the musical direction meaning quietly

explanation.surface: Someone gives a soft cry of oh because they are absolutely delighted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'over the moon' looks like delight, but 'over' reverses the cry, the exclamation and the soft letter, leaving 'the moon' as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Phobos is the larger of the two moons of Mars.

clue.text: Series of analytical returns it's important to see

indicators.note: returns says the run of letters comes back the other way
a series of the word's letters, a consecutive run inside it, is taken

explanation.surface: A run of analytical results that is significant to examine.
explanation.walkthrough: The run YTIC sits inside 'analytical' and 'returns' turns it round. 'see' is a bishop's seat, not looking: a city traditionally has a cathedral.
explanation.definitionFit: A city is traditionally a town with a cathedral, the seat of a bishop's see, so it is a place of importance to a diocese.

clue.text: Drive out character from Dickens novel

parts.note: to drive a car is to steer it
to go out is to go forth

explanation.surface: Chase out a figure from a book by Dickens.
explanation.walkthrough: Steerforth is the charming, reckless friend of the hero in David Copperfield.
explanation.definitionFit: James Steerforth is a character in Charles Dickens's novel David Copperfield.

clue.text: One changing colour making awful sound

indicators.note: sound says the word is taken as it is heard spoken, not as spelt

parts.note: dire means awful or dreadful

explanation.surface: Someone turning pale while making a terrible noise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'making awful sound' reads as one noisy phrase, but 'sound' signals the homophone of DIRE.
explanation.definitionFit: A dyer is a person whose trade is changing the colour of cloth.

clue.text: Chasing policeman with stick, old sailor buckled at the knees

indicators.note: chasing means the later pieces run along behind the officer, following him in the word

parts.note: a bobby is British slang for a police officer
a shaft is a long stick or pole

explanation.surface: Someone with a stick, an old salt with buckled knees, runs after a constable.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition quotes the nursery song: Bobby Shafto went to sea with silver buckles on his knee. A bobby is a British police officer.
explanation.definitionFit: In the English folk song, Bobby Shafto is a sailor who has gone to sea with silver buckles on his knee.

clue.text: Flash bachelor bringing press round

parts.note: a flash is an instant, a mo

explanation.surface: A showy single man pays a visit to the newspapers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'press' is not the newspapers but crowding in, and 'Flash' is a moment, not showy.
explanation.definitionFit: To mob someone is to crowd round them in a throng, pressing close on all sides.

clue.text: Get through threatening times, closing ranks on past

indicators.note: on means the following pieces are attached after the former partner

parts.note: ex means former or past, as in an ex-partner

indicators.note: closing means the two letters close in around the soldiers on either side

parts.note: T is the abbreviation for time, and times gives two of them
T is the abbreviation for time, and times gives two of them
OR stands for other ranks, soldiers who are not officers

explanation.surface: Getting through hard times by pulling together as before.
explanation.walkthrough: 'closing' sets the abbreviation for other ranks (enlisted soldiers) between two time letters, and 'on' adds that after the word for former.
explanation.definitionFit: To extort is to obtain something by threats, getting it through intimidation.

clue.text: Within "peer group" crook at last is exposed

indicators.note: within means the letter is set inside the group of watchers

parts.note: to peer is to stare, so a group of peerers are starers

indicators.note: at last says only the final letter of the word is taken

explanation.surface: A villain is finally unmasked among his own social circle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'peer group' looks like contemporaries but means people who peer: starers. 'Within' puts K, the end of 'crook', inside.
explanation.definitionFit: Starkers is British slang for completely naked, that is, exposed.
